We face delays in a variety of situations. They are either inevitable, e.g., due to system limits, or are intentionally added, e.g., advertisements. In many situations, a visual feedback is provided during the delay to manage expectations. This feedback is usually provided through progress bars, percentages, or countdowns, depending on design limitations such as screen size. In this article, we use 15-second delays and examine (a) how delays affect users’ decision-making and task satisfaction, and (b) how to manipulate time perception to reduce the negative consequences of delays. Experiment 1 (
            N
            =421) shows that faster countdowns increase task satisfaction and lead to more rational decisions in the subsequent task. In Experiment 2, we investigate the effect of countdown speed on delay perception and recall (
            N
            =531). We show that faster countdowns lead to shorter perceived delays, while the delay will be recalled as longer after the task. The opposite is obtained for slower countdowns. We also increased the countdown rate and found a limit for the effect of increased speed. Thus, designers have to trade-off between how delays are perceived at the moment of experience and how they are recalled. We discuss the implications of these findings for user interface design.

result.paraphrase: Delays occur in many contexts, whether unavoidable, such as due to system constraints, or deliberately introduced, such as by advertisements. Often, visual feedback is shown during the wait to set expectations, typically via progress bars, percentages, or countdowns, depending on design constraints like screen size. In this article, we use 15-second delays to study (a) how delays influence users’ decision-making and task satisfaction and (b) how time perception can be manipulated to lessen the negative effects of delays. Experiment 1 (N=421) found that quicker countdowns raise task satisfaction and produce more rational decisions in the follow-up task. In Experiment 2, we examine how countdown speed affects delay perception and recall (N=531). We show that faster countdowns make delays feel shorter, while the delay is later remembered as longer after the task; the reverse pattern appears with slower countdowns. We also increased the countdown rate and identified a limit to the effect of greater speed. Designers therefore must balance how delays are experienced in the moment against how they are remembered. We discuss the implications of these results for user interface design.
